title: Act III, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: Banquo suspects Macbeth 'play'dst most foully' for the crown but hopes the prophecy for his own line will also come true. Macbeth, now king, invites Banquo to the feast and learns he will ride out with Fleance. Alone, Macbeth says 'To be thus is nothing; but to be safely thus': Banquo's royal nature and the prophecy of his heirs torment him, since he holds a 'fruitless crown.' He persuades two murderers that Banquo is their enemy and hires them to kill Banquo and Fleance.

words.sentence:
I am one, my liege,
Whom the vile blows and buffets of the world
Have so incensed that I am reckless what
I do to spite the world.

Do you find
Your patience so predominant in your nature
That you can let this go?

We hear, our bloody cousins are bestow’d
In England and in Ireland, not confessing
Their cruel parricide, filling their hearers
With strange invention: but of that to-morrow,
When therewithal we shall have cause of state
Craving us jointly.

And I another
So weary with disasters, tugg’d with fortune,
That I would set my lie on any chance,
To mend it, or be rid on’t.

There is none but he
Whose being I do fear: and, under him,
My Genius is rebuked; as, it is said,
Mark Antony’s was by Caesar.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “To be thus is nothing; / But to be safely thus” slowly and put it in my own words: Macbeth says that being king is nothing unless he is safely king. Next, craft. I notice the contrast between "thus" and "safely thus." The strongest word is “safely”: it shows his new anxiety about keeping power. Then, effect. Why is being king not enough for Macbeth? My answer: Being king is not enough for Macbeth because he is not safe; his crown brings fear, not peace, so he decides to kill Banquo, whose descendants the witches said would be kings.
